Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run manually) to get the repository ready for CI/CD.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents you’ll need to drop into the repo.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to your GitHub account from here, so the instructions assume you’re running them on your own machine (or a CI runner that has SSH access to the repo).

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you prefer HTTPS, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` and use your GitHub credentials.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install app dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> *Why node:18-alpine?*  
> Alpine images are small, secure, and the latest LTS (18.x) is stable for most Node apps. Adjust the tag if your app requires a different Node version.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s/deployment.yaml` (create the `k8s` folder if it doesn’t exist) with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use Docker Hub or another registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you don’t have a cloud provider
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Tip** – If you’re deploying to a local cluster (e.g., Minikube), change `type: LoadBalancer` to `type: NodePort`.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file named `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'   # match the Docker image

      - name: Cache npm dependencies
        uses: actions/cache@v3
        with:
          path: ~/.npm
          key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
          restore-keys: |
            ${{ runner.os }}-node-

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          echo ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} | docker login ghcr.io -u ${{ github.actor }} --password-stdin
          docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest .
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest

  deploy:
    needs: build-and-test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: production
    steps:
      - name: Checkout source
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up kubectl
        uses: azure/setup-kubectl@v3
        with:
          version: 'latest'

      - name: Apply Kubernetes manifests
        env:
          KUBECONFIG: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
        run: |
          kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
```

> **Secrets you’ll need to add in the repo settings → Secrets → Actions**  
> * `GITHUB_TOKEN` – automatically available; used for pushing to GHCR.  
> * `KUBECONFIG` – a base64‑encoded kubeconfig file that allows the workflow to talk to your cluster.  
>   *If you’re using a cloud provider (EKS, GKE, AKS), you can instead use the provider’s dedicated action (e.g., `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`).*

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically, building the Docker image, pushing it to GitHub Container Registry, and applying the Kubernetes manifests to your cluster.

---

### Quick sanity check

Once the workflow finishes, you can verify:

```bash
# List pods
kubectl get pods -l app=nodejs-welcome

# Get service details
kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome-service
```

If you used `LoadBalancer`, you should see an external IP assigned. If you used `NodePort`, you can access the app via `<minikube-ip>:<node-port>`.

---

## 🎉 Done!

You now have:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys 2 replicas with a LoadBalancer service |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds, tests, pushes, and deploys |

Feel free to tweak the Node version, image registry, or Kubernetes service type to match your environment. Happy coding!
